Let’s dive into Chapter 8: Lean Startup in Established Organizations—Overcoming Barriers.
Now, you might think the Lean Startup approach is just for brand new startups. But here’s the thing—even big companies, nonprofits, and government agencies deal with their own unique hurdles when it comes to innovation. Sure, they often have more resources to work with, but they also wrestle with a lot more inertia and resistance to change.
Trying to introduce Lean Startup principles in these kinds of organizations? It’s a bit like bringing a new species into a well-established ecosystem. You’ve got to make sure the conditions are just right if you want it to thrive.
Let’s talk about some of the most common barriers folks run into.
First, there’s the fear of failure. In a lot of organizations, messing up is seen as something you just can’t do—and that mindset makes it really hard for people to experiment or take any real risks.
Then you’ve got bureaucracy and silos. All those complex approval processes and strict departmental boundaries? They can slow things to a crawl and make it tough for creative ideas to even get off the ground.
And don’t forget the short-term focus. There’s often a lot of pressure to show immediate results, which doesn’t leave much room for investing in long-term learning and real innovation.
So, how do you break through these barriers? There are a few things that really help.
One big move is to create protected spaces for innovation. This could mean dedicated teams or even “innovation labs” where people are encouraged to try new things—and it’s totally okay if they don’t always succeed.
Another key step is to align incentives with learning. In other words, reward teams not just for launching successful projects, but for running experiments and sharing what they learn along the way.
And, of course, it helps a lot to streamline your processes. Simplifying the way new ideas get approved and funded makes it so much easier to test things out quickly.
Here’s a real-world example. Imagine a large retailer wants to launch a brand-new digital service. Instead of sticking to the usual product development routine, they pull together a small, cross-functional team. This team gets its own budget and the power to make decisions on the fly. They jump right into the Build-Measure-Learn loop—testing their ideas with real customers and iterating fast based on feedback. The best ideas get scaled up, and even the failed attempts are seen as valuable learning moments.
Leaders have a huge role to play here. When they openly support experimentation and learning, it sets the tone for everyone else. It can mean challenging some deep-seated beliefs and rethinking what “success” really looks like.
So, what’s the ultimate goal? It’s to weave Lean Startup principles right into the DNA of your organization—making continuous learning and adaptation a natural, everyday part of how things get done.
